s: to grope, pad (walk hesitatingly, especially in the dark)
tappen.et: From Middle High German tāpen with sporadic shortening before /p/ (as in Wappen, Schuppe from Middle High German wāpen, schuope). The verb is of onomatopoeic origin and comparable to the interjection tapp imitating soft walking sounds, though this is attested …

s: tapir (large odd-toed ungulate with long prehensile upper lip)
Tapir.et: Borrowed from French tapir, from Old Tupi tapi'ira.

tapezieren.et: From obsolete tapissieren, borrowed in the 16th century from Middle French tapisser, a derivative of Old French tapiz, from Ancient Greek ταπήτιον (tapḗtion). The modern German form was influenced by the somewhat older noun Tapete and possibly Italian tappezza…

s: wallpaper (paper-like covering applied to interior walls)
Tapete.et: 15th century. From Latin tapēte (“wall hanging cloth”), from tapēs (“carpet”), from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs, “carpet, rug”).

s: brave, dauntless, hardy, tough (strong in the face of hardship, pain, danger)
tapfer.et: From Middle High German tapfer, from Old High German tapfar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz.

s: to tape, to dress or bandage with adhesive tape
tapen.et: From Tape + -en, after English to tape.

s: Wie jung und dumm und hübsch waren ihre Knabengesichter—war wirklich auch er einmal so jung, so täppisch, so hübsch und kindisch gewesen?
täppisch.et: From Middle High German tæpisch, from tāpe (“paw”), from Proto-Germanic *dēbban-, probably related to *dappōn, *dabbōn (“to beat”), itself likely related to the root of English dab (“to press against”), which could be imitative or from a Proto-Indo-European *d…
